newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pensions deal unlikely in German cross-party talks.
newsitem.headline: Pensions deal unlikely in German cross-party talks.

text.p: Germany's government and opposition, still smarting after a bruising encounter on tax reforms, meet again on Tuesday to search for common ground over how to defuse the country's pensions time-bomb.

The omens for a deal did not look good on Monday, however, after the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) rejected Social Security Minister Norbert Bluem's plan to reduce old-age pay in the early decades of the next century.
Bluem has proposed modest cuts in pensions to cope with the "greying" of Germany. The number of pensioners is expected to nearly double to 20 million by 2030.

SPD social affairs spokesman Rudolf Dressler said on Monday his party was joining the exploratory talks to show goodwill. But he added: "If the government sticks to its reduction plans, then there won't be any further negotiations."

Bluem has won approval from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's tripartite coalition for a plan which would eventually reduce a typical pension to 64 percent of average net wages -- a level last seen in the 1970s -- from around 70 percent now.

At the same time, the transfer of around 15 billion marks in non-welfare costs from the state pension fund to the federal budget would enable contributions to be cut from today's record level of 20.3 percent of wages.
Bluem, seeking to honour past pledges that "your pension is safe", has said that old-age pay would not fall in absolute terms in any one year.
But the SPD, in a policy paper issued at the weekend, rejected any cuts whatsoever.

It also called for workers on low wages to pay pensions contributions. The SPD wants 30 billion marks a year in costs -- including the cost of pensions paid to immigrants from the former Soviet Union -- to be borne by the taxpayer.
Both sides are mulling an increase in indirect taxes to pay for the pensions reform.

That would dilute separate coalition plans to cut income and corporate taxes which the SPD has threatened to block in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament after cross-party talks collapsed in acrimony recently.
The SPD does not, however, have the power to block pensions legislation, a policy area which has traditionally been kept out of party politics.
Despite the SPD rebuff, Bluem said he would keep working to achieve a compromise to try and prevent pensions from becoming "a bone of contention" in next year's general election.
"I will not spare any effort for a pensions deal," he told Die Welt newspaper in an interview to be published on Tuesday.
Other coalition leaders were less charitable. "The 'let's carry on' concept of the SPD is no answer," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said, branding the SPD plans as "unfit".
